# Computational Statistics {#sec-Computational_Statistics}
Computational statistics is the intersection of statistics and computing, focusing on methods that use computational power to solve statistical problems. Statistics often rely on analytical solutions and mathematical proofs, whereas computational statistics tackles problems that are analytically intractable or computationally intensive. Perhaps, the most well-known is machine learning and neural networks (see @sec-Neural_Networks).

Machine learning is a subfield of computational statistics and artificial intelligence (AI) that focuses on developing algorithms that can learn patterns from data and make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed for specific tasks. The fundamental premise is that computers can identify patterns in historical data and use these patterns to make informed predictions about new, unseen data. Similarly, the methods in this part will be focused on computational techniques that leverage data to build models, make predictions, and uncover insights, often in ways that traditional statistical methods cannot easily achieve.


## Resampling Methods {#sec-Resampling_Methods}
Resampling techniques form a cornerstone of computational statistics. These methods involve repeatedly drawing samples from observed data to make inferences about population parameters or assess the variability of estimates. The bootstrap (see @sec-Bootstrap) is perhaps the most well-known resampling method, allowing us to estimate standard errors and confidence intervals without making strong parametric assumptions. Cross-validation is another resampling approach used extensively in model selection and validation, particularly in machine learning contexts.

These methods are particularly valuable when the theoretical distribution of a statistic is unknown or difficult to derive. For example, if we want to estimate the standard error of the median from a sample of 50 observations, the bootstrap provides a practical computational solution where analytical methods would be complex.


## Computational Modeling {#sec-Computational_Modeling}
Beyond resampling, computational statistics encompasses sophisticated modeling techniques that learn data patterns. Machine learning represents a major branch of this area, focusing on techniques that can improve their performance through experience. These methods range from relatively simple approaches like decision trees (see @sec-Trees) to complex ensemble methods and support vector machines.

Neural networks (see @sec-Neural_Networks) take this further, using interconnected layers of computational units inspired by neurons to model highly complex relationships. A simple neural network might take input features like temperature and humidity to predict whether it will rain, learning the complex interactions between these variables through an iterative training process.


## Supervised Learning {#sec-Supervised_Learning}
Supervised learning involves training algorithms on labeled data - observations include both input features and a known output. The algorithm learns a mapping from inputs to outputs that can then be applied to new data. For example, given historical data on house characteristics (size, location, number of bedrooms) and their sale prices, a supervised learning algorithm can learn to predict prices for new houses.

Classification and regression are the two main types of supervised learning. Classification predicts categorical outcomes such as whether an email is spam or not, while regression predicts continuous values, like predicting a patient's blood pressure. Linear regression (see @sec-Linear_Regression) and logistic regression (see @sec-Logistic_Regression) are foundational examples of supervised learning methods.


## Unsupervised Learning {#sec-Unsupervised_Learning}
Unsupervised learning works with unlabeled data, seeking to discover hidden structure or patterns without predetermined outcomes. Clustering is a common unsupervised task, where the algorithm groups similar observations together. For instance, a retail company might cluster customers based on purchasing behavior to identify distinct market segments, even without knowing in advance how many segments exist or what defines them.

Dimensionality reduction is another unsupervised technique that transforms high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional representation while preserving important structure. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a classical example, often used to visualize complex datasets or reduce computational burden before applying other methods.
